answer.rationale: The strongest causal signal is temporal: a release shipped 2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing 90m ago, which is consistent with a post-deploy regression rather than pure load. Of the five directions, rollback is the only one that addresses a suspected code cause; failover and capacity treat symptoms and would carry a bad build with them, read-replica routing (memory_b5) helps read-driven primary contention but this is a write-path problem, and a circuit breaker (memory_b4) fits a failing external dependency, not internal latency creep, and would shed exactly the customer writes we are told not to lose. I want memory_b1 verified because it is the single load-bearing precedent for my chosen action and because its summary describes an ERROR spike, not a latency ramp; the archived record will tell me whether the mechanism actually transfers to a write-latency regression, and whether that rollback happened under light traffic rather than at settlement peak. I am deliberately not treating the correlation as proof: 90m of ramp starting 30m after deploy leaves room for a load-driven or saturation cause that peak settlement volume alone could explain, so I hold both hypotheses. Scale is a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout: memory_b6 shows canary cohorts here surface regressions within an hour, so a gated partial rollback both treats and diagnoses, and it bounds the blast radius. Downstream risk flagged explicitly: a rollback during peak heavy writes risks in-flight write loss and possible schema or migration incompatibility with the prior build, so the guarded cohort must drain in-flight writes before cutover and I must confirm the prior build can accept current-schema writes. If the archive shows memory_b1 was an error-rate incident under low traffic with no schema delta, its transfer to this case is weak and I would fall back to add_capacity (memory_b3) as the safer peak-window move.
